The Indian economy is expected to grow by 7.1-7.3 per cent in the current fiscal, with a sustained revival in private investment providing an additional source of demand, Deloitte India said on Friday.
However, geopolitical tensions, volatile energy prices and trade disruptions pose risks to the growth outlook, it added.
Deloitte India Economist Rumki Majumdar said over the past decade, India's growth has rested on resilient household spending and sustained investment push in public infrastructure. Businesses now have better connectivity, healthier balance sheets, and higher capacity utilisation, which strengthens the case for expansion.
"The question is whether these conditions will encourage private investment to play a larger role in boosting growth in the coming years. Recent indicators offer grounds for optimism. articles.title: US proposes ending H-1B deference policy
articles.summary: The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has proposed ending a policy that generally allows immigration officers to rely on earlier approvals when reviewing certain visa extensions. The change could lead to fresh scrutiny of H-1B petitions, more document requests and higher costs for employers.What is the proposed change?The proposal would remove a rule that asks US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) officers to generally respect earlier eligibility decisions when the same parties and facts remain unchanged.Also Read: US ends 540-day automatic work permit extension for immigrants: What changes nowUnder the current policy, officers generally rely on an earlier approval when considering an extension if the circumstances remain the same. They can depart from that decision if they find a significant error, a major change in circumstances or new information that affects eligibility.If the proposal takes effect, officers could reassess each extension request even when the circumstances have not changed. Employers would need to establish that workers continue to meet the requirements for their visa category.Why could H-1B workers be affected?H-1B workers seeking to extend their stay in the US could face closer scrutiny of their petitions. Employers may have to provide additional documents to establish that their employees remain eligible.Also Read: Bahrain’s 90-day temporary work rule explained: What Indian expats need to knowDHS said the existing policy could limit officers' ability to examine cases fully and identify errors or possible fraud. The department said removing the requirement would strengthen checks and ensure employers continue to prove that their workers qualify for the requested immigration benefit.The change could affect H-1B workers from India and other countries, as well as their employers, by subjecting extension petitions to fresh scrutiny. Workers could face additional document requests and delays if USCIS seeks further evidence to verify their eligibility.More paperwork and costs for employersDHS estimates that the change could lead to 6,044 additional requests for evidence (RFEs) each year and cost petitioners about $133,987 annually.An RFE is a notice from USCIS asking an employer or applicant to provide more documents or information before the agency decides a case. Responding to such a notice can increase the time and work involved in an application.The department also warned that more detailed reviews could lengthen processing times and create uncertainty for workers seeking to continue their employment in the US. Additional reviews could increase USCIS's workload and put pressure on its processing resources.The proposed change applies to Form I-129, which employers use to petition for non-immigrant workers. The form covers H-1B petitions as well as several other worker visa categories.The proposal is not a final rule and has not taken effect. DHS is accepting public comments until November 13, 2026, and will consider the feedback before making a final decision.

articles.summary: RIYADH, - The Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen said on Thursday that the country's Houthis had attempted to attack dozens of Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities, as fighting between the Iran-aligned group and Saudi Arabia intensified.The Houthis have been firing ballistic missiles and drones at key Saudi sites for a week, in response to the kingdom's backing of government forces in Yemen's renewed civil war. The coalition's latest statement highlighted the risk to Saudi civilian infrastructure as the conflict escalated.Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said at a press conference that the Houthis had launched 20 attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh this month, killing 17 people and wounding 333 others. The airport, one of Saudi Arabia's main international aviation hubs, was among the civilian infrastructure targeted in what the coalition described as a series of attacks.The coalition also said Houthi attacks on Abha airport, in southwestern Saudi Arabia near the Yemeni border, had killed three people and wounded 28.Maliki said the Houthis had acquired advanced military technology with the help of "regional actors," including ballistic missiles, drones and explosive-laden fast boats.The spokesperson also said the coalition had destroyed 127 weapons storage facilities and launch platforms in Yemen's mountainous areas.He called on the Houthis to immediately halt operations targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure, and said the group should read the coalition's statement carefully and "between the lines."Shortly after the coalition's statement, the Houthi military spokesperson said Saudi airspace and airports were unsafe, renewing a warning to airlines while excluding airspace over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.Yemen has been mired in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention the following year. The UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted major fighting, and a de facto truce held even after it expired six months later. But efforts to turn it into a lasting political settlement have stalled as regional tensions have intensified.

India's current account deficit narrowed to USD 5.2 billion in August from USD 6.1 billion a year ago, aided by a lower merchandise trade deficit and higher surpluses in services trade, according to preliminary data released by the RBI on Thursday.
The net deficit in the merchandise trade account declined to USD 26.6 billion in August from USD 27.6 billion in the same month last year.
Merchandise exports rose to USD 44.7 billion in August from USD 35.1 billion a year ago, while imports increased to USD 71.3 billion from USD 62.7 billion, the RBI data showed.
The surplus in services trade increased to USD 16.5 billion in August from USD 15.6 billion a year ago. Services exports rose to USD 35.5 billion from USD 31.2 billion, while imports increased to USD 18.9 billion from USD 15.6 billion.
Net transfers, including remittances, increased to USD 12.8 billion in August from USD 12.2 billion a year ago, while the net deficit in the income account widened to USD 8 billion from USD 6.3 .

articles.summary: RBI has deployed an estimated $75 bn-$80 bn through spot dollar sales and currency swaps since June, as high oil prices, rising US Treasury yields and foreign equity outflows weigh on the rupee

articles.title: Big surge! Early Diwali for Sensex, Nifty as stock market skyrockets on Reliance Jio IPO, IT shares jump - More to come?
articles.summary: Indian benchmarks rallied more than 2% on Thursday, with the Sensex topping 74,330 and the Nifty reclaiming 23,000. Strong IT earnings, buying in financial and consumer stocks, a firmer rupee and lower oil prices supported sentiment despite weakness in Asian markets.
